unit.title: Perform hair shaping on excessively curly hair

summary: This unit teaches you to cut and shape very tightly curled (coily) hair with clippers, trimmers and scissors: fades and tapers, rounded afros, high-tops and crisp line-ups. You will learn to consult the client, check the scalp and skin for razor bumps, keloids and infections, allow for shrinkage, look after your clippers, deal with a nick hygienically, and give aftercare advice that suits coily hair.

blocks.p: This unit is about cutting and shaping **excessively curly hair**: hair that grows in very tight coils or kinks. It is the hair of most of the clients who sit in a Jamaican barber's or stylist's chair, so this is everyday work, and work that clients judge closely. A fade that is uneven or a hairline pushed back a centimetre is seen by everyone the client meets for the next three weeks.

Very curly hair does not behave like straight hair. It shrinks, it hides its real length, it is dry and fragile, and when it is cut too close it can curl back into the skin and cause bumps. The unit is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and covers men's, women's and children's cuts.

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and two group practical tasks: a rounded afro shaped on picked-out hair, and a mid fade with blended guard lines and a natural line-up. The assessor watches your consultation, safety, method, balance checks and clean-up, not only the finished cut.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph the hair and the work area. Do not show a model's face unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Straight hair grows from a straight follicle and is round in cross-section. Very curly hair grows from a **curved follicle** and is flattened, like a ribbon. It leaves the scalp already bending and winds into tight coils or zigzag kinks.
Each bend is a weak point, so coily hair **breaks easily**, above all when it is dry or combed roughly.
The scalp's natural oil (sebum) cannot travel easily round the bends, so the hair is often **dry** even when the scalp is oily.
The coils wrap around each other, so the hair **tangles and mats**, and tiny knots form on single strands.
Because the cut end of a coiled hair is sharp and points back towards the skin, close cutting can lead to **ingrown hairs** (see 'Consultation and skin and scalp checks').

blocks.h: What to judge before you cut

head: Feature
What it means
Why it matters for the cut
rows: Curl pattern
How tight the coil is: loose curls, tight coils or zigzag kinks. One head often has two or three patterns.
Tighter areas shrink more and look shorter, so the same guard can look uneven. The crown and nape often differ from the sides.
Shrinkage
How much shorter the hair looks in its coiled state than when it is stretched out.
You must cut for the length the client will **see**, not the stretched length. You can cut more off, but you cannot add it back.
Density
How many hairs grow on each part of the scalp (thick or thin hair).
Dense hair holds a round afro or high-top well. Thin areas look patchy when cut very short and need a longer guard.
Texture
The thickness of each single hair: fine, medium or coarse.
Fine coily hair is the most fragile. Coarse hair resists the clipper and needs sharp, well-oiled blades.
Condition
Dry, brittle, matted, or soft and moisturised; natural, coloured or relaxed.
Dry, matted hair must be detangled gently first. Damaged ends may need to come off.
Growth direction (the grain)
The direction the hair lies as it leaves the scalp. It changes at the crown, the nape and the hairline.
Cutting against the grain cuts closer; cutting with it leaves the hair a little longer and is kinder to bump-prone skin.
Hairline and head shape
Where the natural hairline sits; flat areas, bumps, dents and scars on the head.
The line-up follows the natural hairline. Length is left where it balances a flat area or covers a scar.

blocks.p: Take one coil at the crown, stretch it gently and let it go. If it stretches to about 8 cm and springs back to about 3 cm, more than half of its length is hidden. Tightly coiled hair commonly looks **half its real length or less**, and it shrinks most when it dries after washing.

ul: Shrinkage is not a fault. It is a sign of healthy, springy hair.
Hair that has been blown out, pressed or silk-pressed is stretched. After the next wash it **reverts**: it curls up again and looks much shorter, and often uneven if it was cut while straight.
Wet hair is also stretched by the weight of the water. A small trim on wet coily hair can turn out far shorter than the client wanted once it dries.
So: cut the hair in the state the client wears it, take off less than you think, and check before you take more.

blocks.note: Do the stretch test where the client can see it in the mirror. It explains in five seconds why you are leaving the top a little longer than the length he first asked for.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Clipper and trimmer blades
Nicks and cuts; blood-borne infection
Check the blades are set correctly before every client
Keep the skin held firm and use light pressure
Never cut over bumps, moles, sores or keloids
Dirty tools
Ringworm, impetigo, folliculitis and other infections passed from client to client
Brush off the hair, then disinfect, between all clients
Fresh neck strip and clean cape for each client
Electricity
Shock, burns, fire
Check the cord, plug and charger before use
Dry hands; keep cords away from water and walkways
Take damaged tools out of use
Hot blades
Burns to the client's skin
Oil the blades; feel the blade on your own wrist during long cuts
Use coolant spray or change clippers if it runs hot
Cut hair on the floor
Slips; a dirty, unprofessional shop
Sweep up between clients into a covered bin
Scissors
Cuts to you or the client
Carry and pass them closed, handles first
Never put them in a pocket
Standing and bending
Back, neck and shoulder strain
Raise or lower the chair so you work at chest height
Move your feet around the client; do not twist

blocks.h: Checking your clippers before you start

ul: **The blades.** A clipper has a fixed (still) blade and a moving (cutting) blade. The teeth of the moving blade must sit a little **behind** the teeth of the fixed blade, as the maker's instructions show. If the moving blade sticks out past the fixed blade it will cut or nick the client's skin. Check this every day, and again if the clippers are dropped.
**Teeth.** A broken or bent tooth scratches the scalp. Replace the blade.
**Guards.** A cracked guard, or one with a missing tooth, can slip or let the blade through and leave a bald patch. Throw it away. Press each guard on until it clicks.
**Cord, plug and charger.** No cracks, bare wire, loose pins or tape repairs.
**Sound and feel.** Clippers that rattle, pull the hair or run hot usually need cleaning and oiling. If that does not cure it, the blade is blunt or out of line: have it sharpened, replaced or reset.

blocks.note: If a tool has a cracked plug, a taped or frayed cord or a damaged casing, stop using it, label it 'Do not use', and report it. Never 'make it last one more cut'.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: Jamaica's mains supply is 110 V, or 220 V for some equipment, at 50 Hz. Read the label on the clippers or the charger and check that it matches the socket. Clippers bought abroad may be made for a different voltage or for 60 Hz, and can run badly, overheat or burn out here.
blocks.label: Jamaica

flow: Switch off and take off the guard
Brush all the hair out of the teeth and the guard
Spray or wipe the blades and guard with clipper disinfectant
Leave it wet for the contact time on the label
Wipe dry
Put a drop or two of clipper oil on the blades and run them for a few seconds
Wipe off the extra oil
Check the blade setting

ul: **Hair comes off first.** Disinfectant cannot work through hair and grease.
Use a disinfectant made for clippers, as its maker says. If there was blood, use one that works against blood-borne germs and give it the full contact time.
**Oil** keeps the blades cool, sharp and smooth. Use clipper oil, not hair oil or cooking oil, which gum up the blades.
Combs, picks, brushes and guards are washed in warm soapy water, then disinfected for the label's contact time, rinsed, dried and stored covered.

A **twist sponge** cannot be properly disinfected between clients, because hair and product stay in the holes. Follow the Centre's rule: many shops keep one sponge per client or ask clients to bring their own.
At the end of the day: clean more fully, take the blade off if the maker allows, check cords and chargers, and store tools dry and covered.

flow: Stop cutting; tell the client calmly and apologise
Put on disposable gloves
Press a clean, single-use pad on the nick until the bleeding stops
If needed, apply single-use styptic powder or liquid on a disposable applicator
Offer a small plaster
Put the pad, applicator and gloves in a sealed bag, as the Centre's rules say
Clean, then disinfect, the tool before it is used again
Wash your hands
Record it in the accident book

ul: **Styptic** is a product that stops bleeding from a small nick. Never use a shared styptic pencil: it carries one client's blood to the next.
Blood can carry infections such as hepatitis B and HIV, so treat all blood as infectious.
A used razor blade goes straight into a **sharps box**: a closed, puncture-proof container. Never into the ordinary bin.
If the cut is deep or will not stop bleeding, get first-aid help.

sections.title: Consultation and skin and scalp checks

blocks.p: Talk before you cut. Seat the client, look at him in the mirror with the hair as he normally wears it, and agree the cut. Then check the scalp and skin, before the cape hides the neck.

head: Ask or check
Why it matters
rows: What style, and how short? (Use pictures.)
'Low', 'a trim' and 'a fade' mean different things to different people. A picture settles it.
How do you wear it each day: picked out, brushed down, sponged or twisted?
The cut must suit how he styles it. An afro is cut picked out; waves are cut with the grain and brushed down.
What was used last time? (Guard numbers; the record card.)
Lets you repeat a cut he liked, or go one step shorter or longer.
Do you get bumps after a haircut or shave? Any scars that grow?
Points to razor bumps and keloids, where you must not cut close.
Work, school and upkeep
Some schools and jobs set rules on hair length and designs. A sharp fade needs a visit every two to three weeks.
How long since it was washed? Any products in it?
Grease, gel and sand clog and blunt the blades. Hair is cut clean and dry.
A child: is the parent or guardian present and agreed?
The adult agrees the style and is told about anything you find.

head: Feature
What usually suits
rows: Round face
Some height on top and shorter sides, to make the face look longer. A high or mid fade helps.
Long, narrow face
Less height on top and some fullness at the sides. A low fade or taper keeps the width.
Square face, strong jaw
Most short styles. Slightly rounded corners on the line-up soften the look.
Oval face
Almost any style.
Flat crown or back of the head
Leave a little more length there to round the shape.
Bumps, dents or scars on the scalp
A longer guard over the area; avoid a skin-close fade there.
Thin or receding areas
Avoid very short fades that show them up, and never 'draw in' a new hairline by cutting it back.
Dense hair
Holds a round afro, a tapered afro or a high-top well.
Little time for upkeep; outdoor work
A low, even cut or a simple taper.

blocks.p: Give your advice and the reason for it, then let the client choose. Agree the final length, the fade height and the price before you start. If, partway through, you think a different length would look better, **stop and ask**. Never change the plan on your own.

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Razor bumps (pseudofolliculitis barbae, PFB)
Small red or dark bumps on the beard line, neck or nape, where cut hairs have curled back into the skin or grown sideways under it.

Not contagious. Do not cut down to the skin there: use a guard, cut with the grain and keep the trimmer light. Never pick or squeeze. If bumps are swollen or full of pus, do not cut over them; suggest a doctor.
Firm bumps and raised scars at the nape (often called 'barber's bumps')
Small, firm bumps along the back hairline that can join into thick, raised scars. Close cutting and rubbing collars make them worse.
Avoid cutting close there: leave the nape longer and soft, no bare-skin line. Suggest he sees a doctor.
Keloid
A thick, raised, shiny scar that has grown bigger than the wound that caused it, often behind the ear, at the nape or on the jaw.
Never cut over or nick a keloid: any injury can make it grow. Work around it with a guard. Suggest a doctor if it is growing.
Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis)
Round, scaly patches with broken hairs or bald spots. A fungal infection, common in children.
**Contagious. Do not cut.** Politely refer the client (or parent) to a doctor.
Head lice
Small insects; tiny eggs (nits) glued to the hairs near the scalp; itching.
**Contagious. Do not cut.** Tell the client or parent in private and suggest a pharmacist or doctor.
Impetigo; infected follicles (folliculitis)
Weeping sores with honey-coloured crusts; red, painful pus spots around the hairs.
**Do not cut.** Refer to a doctor.
Traction alopecia
Thinning or bald areas at the hairline from tight braids, ponytails or constant pulling.
Not contagious. Cut gently, do not take the line-up back into the thin area, and advise looser styles.
Dandruff or a dry scalp
Loose white flakes; no redness or sores.
Carry on. Advise on washing and moisturising the scalp.
Cuts, scabs, moles and skin tags
Broken or raised skin.
Do not cut over them. Work around with a guard, or postpone if the area is large or looks infected.

blocks.note: You are not a doctor. Do not name a disease to the client. Say what you have seen, quietly and in private, explain why you cannot cut today or cannot cut close, and suggest a doctor. Afterwards, clean and disinfect everything the client touched.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Why very curly hair gets razor bumps

blocks.p: A curly hair that is cut very close, or cut against the grain with the skin stretched, is left with a sharp tip at or below the skin's surface. As it grows, its natural curve turns it back **into the skin**, and the body reacts as it would to a splinter: a sore, itchy bump. Repeated bumps can leave dark marks and scars. The cure is not a closer cut. It is a slightly longer one, with the grain.
Write what you agreed and what you found on the client's **record card**, with the guard numbers and lever setting, so that the cut can be repeated next visit.

head: Tool
What it is for
rows: Clippers
Removing bulk and cutting fades and tapers, with or without a guard.
Guards (attachment combs)
Plastic combs that clip onto the clippers to leave the hair at a set length.
Trimmers (outliners), often with a T-shaped blade
Fine work at the hairline: line-ups, around the ears, the nape, parts and detail. The T-blade is wider than the body, so you can see the corner and make a crisp outline.
Afro pick
A comb with long, wide-spaced teeth for lifting the hair out from the scalp and shaping an afro.
Wide-tooth comb
Detangling, and lifting and spreading the hair for clipper-over-comb and scissor-over-comb work.
Cutting scissors
Scissor-over-comb shaping of afro outlines, and removing single long hairs.
Soft brush
Brushing short hair in the direction of growth to see lines in a fade; removing loose hair from the neck.
Twist sponge
A sponge with holes, rubbed in small circles over short coily hair to form small coils or twists.
Neck strip
A paper strip between the client's neck and the cape: it keeps the cape off the skin and stops cut hair falling into the collar.
Cape
Covers the client's clothes.
Hand mirror
Shows the client the back and sides.
Blade brush, clipper disinfectant and clipper oil
Cleaning and caring for the clippers between clients.
Single-use styptic, gloves and pads
Dealing with a nick.

blocks.p: The number on a guard tells you **how long the hair is left**. On most clippers, a higher number leaves the hair longer. The usual set is in steps of about 3 mm, but makes differ: check the chart that came with your clippers.

head: Guard
Hair left (typical)
Common use on coily hair
rows: No guard, lever closed
Very close to the skin
The lowest band of a skin-close fade. Not for bump-prone skin.
About 1.5 mm
Low in a fade; blending between no guard and #1.
About 3 mm
A low, even cut; the lower bands of a fade.
About 4.5 mm
Blending between #1 and #2.
About 6 mm
Short sides; the upper band of a fade; a low cut on top.
About 10 mm
A short top; the base of a taper.
About 13 mm
A fuller top that still looks neat.
About 16 mm to 25 mm
Longer tops and removing bulk before shaping.

ul: To go a little shorter, drop one guard number; to leave more, go up one. Change one step at a time.
Because coily hair shrinks, a guard leaves it **looking** shorter than the same guard on straight hair. Pick the hair out before you judge.
The same guard cuts closer **against** the grain than **with** it.

blocks.p: Many clippers have a **lever (taper lever)** on the side. It slides the moving blade to open or close the blade a little. **Closed** gives the closest cut. **Open** leaves the hair slightly longer: on many clippers the difference between closed and open is about half a guard step. This gives you in-between lengths without changing guards, which is how the lines of a fade are blended.

blocks.note: Blade lengths, guard sizes and the amount the lever moves are different from maker to maker. Follow the maker's chart and your instructor, and test a new clipper on a training head before you use it on a client.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Preparing the client and the hair

flow: Wash your hands
Ask the client to remove caps, chains and earrings that are in the way
Wrap a fresh neck strip snugly round the neck
Fasten the cape over it so that only the strip touches the skin
Fold the top of the strip down over the cape
Check it is snug but comfortable
Adjust the chair height

ul: A **snug neck strip** is what keeps short, sharp bits of coily hair from falling into the collar. They itch, and on the neck they can cause bumps.
Use a **fresh strip for each client**. A reused strip, or a cape that touches one neck after another, can spread germs.
Shake out or change the cape between clients.

blocks.h: Dry and picked out, stretched, or wet?

head: State of the hair
What you see
Use it when
rows: Dry and picked out
The real shape and length the client wears every day. Uneven areas show up.
Afros, tapers, fades, high-tops: almost all clipper and shaping work on coily hair.
Stretched: blown out or pressed
A smooth, even line while the hair stays straight.
Clients who wear the hair pressed or blown out. Take off less, and warn that it may look shorter and uneven when it reverts.
Wet
The hair hangs longer under the weight of the water, then shrinks as it dries.
Not for shaping coily hair. Used only for some scissor trims by an experienced stylist.

flow: Check the hair is clean and dry
Divide tangled hair into small sections
Hold the section near the scalp to take the pull
Work from the ends towards the scalp with fingers, then a wide-tooth comb
Mist very lightly with water or leave-in if the hair is brittle
Pick the hair out from the scalp evenly all over
Pat the shape lightly and look for uneven areas

ul: **Ends first.** Starting at the roots pushes the knots together and tears the hair out.
Never rake a fine-tooth comb through coily hair.
Matted areas, often at the back where the head rubs a pillow or headrest, are worked loose a little at a time. Do not cut out a mat without asking the client.
Pick out **evenly**. If one side is picked out more than the other, you will cut the shape lopsided.
If the hair is full of grease, gel or sand, it should be washed and dried first. Dirty hair blunts and clogs the blades.
The client sits upright, back against the chair, feet on the footrest, **head level**. A tilted head gives a tilted cut.
Move the head gently with your fingertips and say what you need: 'Head forward for me, please.'
For the nape, ask him to bend his head **forward**. This stretches and flattens the skin at the back of the neck so the outline is clean and the trimmer does not catch in a skin fold.
For around the ear, fold the ear down gently with your free hand.
Stand so that the area you are cutting is at about chest height, and step round the chair instead of leaning over the client.
Hold the clippers lightly, with the flat of the blade or guard resting on the head. Let the blades do the cutting; do not press.
**Against the grain** (against the direction of growth) lifts the hair into the blade and gives the closest, most even cut. This is the usual way to cut bulk and fades on coily hair.
**With the grain** leaves the hair a little longer and lies it down. Use it for waves, for a softer finish, and on skin that gets bumps.
Work in overlapping strokes so that no strip is missed. Go over each area more than once: coils spring up after the first pass.
**Flicking out** (a scooping or 'C' stroke): as the clippers travel up the head, rock your wrist so the blade arcs away from the scalp. The stroke ends in a soft edge instead of a hard line.
**Clipper-over-comb**: lift the hair with a wide-tooth comb and run the clippers across the comb. Used to soften the top of a fade and to shape longer hair.
Brush or pick the hair as you go. You cannot judge a blend through loose clippings.

head: Word
What it means
rows: Fade
The sides and back go gradually from longer hair down to very short hair or bare skin near the hairline, with no visible line.
Skin fade (bald fade)
A fade that goes right down to the skin at the bottom.
Low fade
The shortest band stays low: just above the ear and round the nape.
Mid fade
The fade line sits about halfway up the sides, around the level of the temples.
High fade
The fade line sits high, near where the head starts to curve in towards the top.
Taper
The hair is shortened gradually only at the sideburns and the nape. The rest of the sides stays fuller.
Fade line (guideline)
The level line you cut first, all round the head, to mark where one length changes to the next.
Blending
Removing the lines between the bands so the length changes smoothly.

flow: Consult: agree the top length and where the fade sits; record the guards
Pick out the hair
Remove bulk on the top and sides with the longest guard agreed
Set the fade line about halfway up the sides with a shorter guard, level all round
Cut the band below it with a shorter guard again, closer to the hairline
Blend each line: open and close the lever, flick out, or use the in-between guard
Soften the top line with clipper-over-comb if needed
Brush off and check both sides in the mirror
Line up the edges with trimmers
Remove loose hair and show the client

ul: **Longest guard first.** If you slip with a long guard there is still hair to correct it with. Work from long to short, top to bottom.
**Set the line level.** Use fixed points on both sides, such as the top of each ear or the corner of each temple, and check from the front and from the back.
Each band is narrow: usually one to two finger-widths. Wide bands leave no room to blend.

**To blend a line** between two guards, attack the line itself, not the areas above and below it. For example, between a #1 band and a #2 band: use the #1 with the lever open, or a #1.5, in short flicking strokes just across the line, until it disappears.
Stretch the skin flat with your free hand over curves and behind the ear.

A dark patch means hair is still too long there; a light patch means it has been cut too short. Fix a dark patch by cutting it; fix a light patch only by taking the area around it very slightly shorter, or leave it and note it.
On bump-prone skin, or over bumps and scars at the nape, do not fade to skin. Stop at a guard and keep the hairline soft.
Stand directly **behind** the client and compare the two sides in the mirror; then look from the **front**. The fade lines should sit at the same height on both sides.
Check the back from each side: the fade should run level round the head, not dip or climb, unless a drop was agreed.
Brush the hair down and look in good light for lines and patches.
Use the hand mirror to show the client the back before you finish.

blocks.note: Rushing the blend is the commonest fault. If a line will not go, stop, brush the hair, and work out which side of the line is too long before you cut again. Cutting higher and higher to chase a line turns a mid fade into a high one the client did not ask for.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Afros, high-tops and other curly shapes

flow: Consult: agree the size of the round shape
Detangle the dry hair in sections, ends first
Pick it out evenly all over, so it stands at its full length
Start at the nape and sides
Cut the outline with scissors or clippers over a wide-tooth comb, in an even curve
Work up to the crown and top, a little at a time
Pick out again and remove the long hairs that appear
Check the balance from the front, back and both sides
Finish with a light line-up and a moisturiser

ul: The finished outline is **an even curve all round the head**, following the round of the skull: no corners, flat spots or dips.

**Scissor-over-comb or clipper-over-comb** gives the neatest outline: the comb lifts and holds the hair, and the blades trim what stands beyond it. Keep the comb moving and angled to follow the curve.
Some barbers shape freehand, with the clippers held away from the head. This takes a steady hand; start with the comb.
**Take off a little at a time.** You can cut more, but you cannot put length back.
**Pick out again** after each round of cutting. Cutting presses hair down, and coils that were bent over stand up as long hairs when picked.
Check with the client's **head upright** and level. Stand behind and compare both sides in the mirror, look from the front, and look at the profile from each side.
Step back. A shape is judged from a metre or two away, not from 20 cm.

head: Style
What it is
Points to watch
rows: Low, even cut
One guard all over, with a line-up.
Go over it several times in different directions; coils hide from the first pass.
Tapered afro
A round or oval top with the sides and nape tapered shorter.
Blend the taper into the afro with clipper-over-comb so there is no step.
High-top (flat-top)
Short or faded sides with tall hair on top, cut flat across.
Needs dense hair. Pick the top out fully, then level it with clippers over a comb or freehand, checking from the front and the side that it is flat and not sloping.
Short tapered cut for women
Short, shaped sides and nape with soft length on top.
Leave the top a little longer than asked at first; shrinkage will shorten it. Keep the hairline soft.
Waves
A low cut brushed flat so the coils lie in a wave pattern.
Cut **with** the grain with a low guard, so the pattern is not cut out.
Sponge twists or coils
Short hair formed into small coils with a twist sponge.
The hair needs some length (about a #4 or longer) and a little moisturiser. Rub in small circles in one direction.
A part (a cut-in line)
A thin line cut into the hair as a side part or design.
Comb or mark the line first. Use the corner of the trimmer **lightly**, in short strokes; do not press into the scalp, and keep it narrow.

blocks.h: Trimming hair that is worn straight

blocks.p: A client with a blow-out or silk press may ask for a trim. The line you cut will be smooth today, but warn her before you start: after her next wash the hair will curl up and look much shorter, and it may not sit evenly. Take off less than she asks, agree the length while she watches, and note on her card that the hair was cut stretched.

blocks.note: Some schools and workplaces have rules about hair length, fades, parts and designs. For a school-age client, ask what the school allows before you cut a part or a design.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **line-up** (also called a shape-up or edge-up) is a sharp outline at the front hairline, the temples, the sideburns, around the ears and the nape. It is usually the **last** part of the cut: the outline and detail are finished after the bulk, the shape and the blend.

flow: Check the trimmers: clean, disinfected, oiled, blade set safely
Brush the hairline into place and find the natural line
Ask the client to keep still
Hold the skin slightly firm with your free hand
Front: start at the centre and work out to each side with the corner of the blade, in short, light strokes
Temples: turn the corner cleanly
Sideburns: level them against each other
Around the ears: fold the ear down
Nape: head bent forward
Check both sides match
Brush away loose hair

ul: **Follow the natural hairline.** Take off only the stray hairs outside it. Every line-up that cuts back into the hairline moves it a little further back, and over months the forehead looks higher and the edges thin.
**Hold the skin slightly firm** so the trimmer glides over a flat surface and does not catch in a fold.
Use the blade flat and light. Digging the corner in cuts the skin and causes bumps.
The **temples** are the flat areas at each side of the forehead, where the front line turns down towards the sideburns.
The **sideburns** are the hair growing down the sides of the face in front of the ears. Check their length against a fixed point on each side, such as the middle of the ear.
The nape can be squared, rounded or tapered (faded out). A tapered nape grows out most neatly and is the kindest to bump-prone skin.
Some barbers finish the outline with a razor. That needs a fresh single-use blade for each client and a sharps box, and it is not done on skin that gets bumps.
Remove loose hair from the face, ears and neck with a clean soft brush or towel.
Coily hair is dry and fragile, so finish with a **light leave-in conditioner or moisturiser**, a little at a time. Heavy grease blocks the scalp and attracts dust.
Style as agreed: pick out, brush, or form coils with the twist sponge.
Strong alcohol splashes sting and dry the skin; on freshly lined skin use a mild, soothing product if anything.
Take off the cape and neck strip carefully so hair does not fall into the collar.
Hold the hand mirror so the client can see the back and both sides. **The cut is finished when he has seen it and agreed the result**, not before.

head: Advice
Why
rows: Moisturise the hair and scalp with a light moisturiser or leave-in.
Coily hair dries out easily, and dry hair breaks.
Use a soft brush, a pick or a sponge gently. Do not rake a fine comb through it.
Rough combing snaps the coils.
Sleep in a satin or silk cap, or on a satin pillowcase.
Keeps the shape and the moisture; cotton rubs and dries the hair.
If you get bumps: no very close cuts or shaves, nothing against the grain, and do not pick or squeeze.
Close cutting lets the hair curl back into the skin; picking causes infection and scars.
See a doctor if bumps become painful or infected, or a scar keeps growing.
These need medical care, not a barber.
Protect a newly bared scalp, neck and ears from strong sun with a hat.
Skin that was covered by hair burns easily.
Come back in about two to three weeks for a line-up or fade, or as the style needs.
Coily hair grows out of a sharp shape quickly.

flow: Sweep up the cut hair into a covered bin
Bin the neck strip; shake out or change the cape
Brush, disinfect and oil the clippers and trimmers
Wash and disinfect combs, picks, guards and brushes
Wipe the chair, headrest and work top
Wash your hands
Fill in the record card

blocks.p: On a busy Saturday, hair builds up round the chair quickly. Sweep **between clients**, not only at the end of the day: hair on a tiled floor is slippery, and it looks dirty to the next client.

head: What to record
Example
rows: Date and client
07/11/2026, Mr D. Francis, Portmore
Hair and scalp
Dense, tight coils, dry; mild bumps at the nape, no infection seen
Style agreed
Mid fade, soft tapered nape, natural line-up
Guards and lever
Top #4; sides #2, then #1; lever open to blend; nape left at #1, no skin
Products
Light leave-in moisturiser
Advice given
No close cuts at the nape; see a doctor if bumps worsen; return in 2 to 3 weeks
Any accident or reaction
None

ul: I can explain what excessively curly hair is and why it is dry, fragile and quick to tangle.
I can explain shrinkage and how it changes the way I cut.
I can check clippers, guards, cords and plugs, and say what to do with a damaged tool.
I can clean, disinfect and oil clippers and trimmers in the right order.
I can deal with a nick: gloves, a clean pad, single-use styptic, safe disposal and a record.
I can carry out a consultation and choose a style for the face, head shape, density and lifestyle.
I can recognise razor bumps, keloids, ringworm, head lice and traction alopecia, and say when to refer and when to adapt the cut.
I can explain why very curly hair gets razor bumps and how to cut for a client who gets them.
I can name the tools and say what guard numbers and the lever do.
I can gown a client with a neck strip, and detangle and pick out the hair from the ends.
I can compare cutting dry and picked out with cutting stretched or wet.
I can describe the steps of a mid fade and three ways to blend a line.
I can check that a fade is level on both sides.
I can shape a rounded afro and check its balance.
I can describe a high-top, a taper, waves and sponge twists.
I can do a line-up that follows the natural hairline and explain why.
I can finish the cut, give aftercare advice, clean up and fill in a record card.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I remove bulk with the longest guard first, so that a slip can still be corrected.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Excessively curly hair
Hair that grows in very tight coils or kinks.
Shrinkage
The way coily hair springs back and looks much shorter than its stretched length.
Reverting
Stretched or pressed hair curling up again after washing.
Density
How many hairs grow on each part of the scalp.
Grain
The direction in which the hair grows.
Guard
The plastic attachment clipped onto clippers to leave the hair at a set length.
Lever (taper lever)
The lever on the side of clippers that opens or closes the blade a little.
Trimmers (outliners)
Small clippers, often with a T-blade, for outlines and detail.
Afro pick
A comb with long, wide-spaced teeth used to lift and shape an afro.
Twist sponge
A holed sponge rubbed over short coily hair to form small coils or twists.
Neck strip
A paper strip worn round the neck under the cape, fresh for each client.
Fade
A cut where the sides go gradually from longer hair down to very short hair or bare skin.
Taper
Gradual shortening at the sideburns and nape only.
Fade line (guideline)
The level line cut first to mark where the length changes.
Blending
Removing the lines between lengths so the change is smooth.
Flicking out
Rocking the clippers away from the head at the end of a stroke to leave a soft edge.
Clipper-over-comb
Cutting hair that is lifted and held by a comb, with clippers.
Scissor-over-comb
Cutting hair that is lifted and held by a comb, with scissors.
Line-up (shape-up, edge-up)
A sharp outline at the front, temples, sideburns and nape.
Temples
The flat areas at each side of the forehead, where a line-up turns a corner.
Sideburns
The hair that grows down the sides of the face in front of the ears.
Nape
The back of the neck, where the hairline ends.
High-top
A style with short sides and tall, flat hair on top.
Razor bumps (PFB)
Bumps caused by cut hairs curling back into the skin; pseudofolliculitis barbae.
Keloid
A thick, raised scar that grows bigger than the wound that caused it.
Ringworm (tinea capitis)
A contagious fungal scalp infection with round, scaly patches and broken hairs.
Traction alopecia
Hair loss caused by tight styles or constant pulling.
Styptic
A single-use powder or liquid that stops bleeding from a small nick.
Sharps box
A closed, puncture-proof container for used razor blades.
Contact time
How long a tool must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
Record card
The client's record of the cut, guards, products, advice and any problems.

c1.title: A mid fade before prize-giving in Half Way Tree
c1.text: Jaheim Morrison, 15, comes to a barber shop in Half Way Tree, Kingston, with his mother for a cut before his school's prize-giving. He has dense, tightly coiled hair and wants a mid fade with the top left at a #4. Trainee barber Kemar removes the bulk, sets the fade line with a #2 and cuts the band below it with a #1. A clear line now shows between the #1 and #2 bands, and the fade line looks higher above the left ear than above the right. Jaheim also asks for two lines cut in above his ear.

c2.title: A police officer's neckline in Morant Bay
c2.text: Corporal Leroy Stewart, 41, has his hair cut every two weeks at a shop in Morant Bay, St Thomas. He asks for his usual: 'skin at the back and a sharp line'. Trainee Akeem sees a row of small, firm bumps along the back hairline, and two of them have joined into a thick, raised scar. One bump near the left ear is swollen and has a yellow head. Mr Stewart says his uniform collar rubs the area and that the bumps 'come up after every trim'.

c3.title: A rounded afro for graduation in Santa Cruz
c3.text: Shantelle Powell, 22, graduates on Saturday and wants her natural hair shaped into a neat, rounded afro at a salon in Santa Cruz, St Elizabeth. She took out her braids yesterday. Her hair is clean and dry, but matted at the back, and it stands higher on the right side than on the left. She says, 'Just shape it. Please don't take off much.' Trainee Monique is doing the cut.

c4.title: From a blow-out to curls in Lucea
c4.text: Mrs Andrea Samuels, 35, has worn her coily hair blown out straight for years. Today, at a salon in Lucea, Hanover, her hair is freshly blown out and reaches her chin. She has decided to wear it curly from now on and wants a short tapered cut with 'about 5 cm of curl' on top. Trainee Kimone stretches one coil from an unstraightened patch at the nape: it measures about 9 cm stretched and about 4 cm when let go.

c5.title: Friday evening at a shop in Spanish Town
c5.text: It is Friday evening at a busy barber shop in Spanish Town, St Catherine, and six clients are waiting. Trainee Tyrese drops his clippers on the tiled floor. They still run. The #2 guard now has a crack along one side. His last client's hair is still in the blades, and a pile of hair has built up around the chair. During a line-up, his trimmer nicks the next client's temple and a spot of blood gets onto the blade.

questions.q: How should Kemar remove the line between the #1 band and the #2 band?
o: Go over the whole #2 band again with the #1 guard, lever closed
Work across the line with the #1 and the lever open, flicking out
Cut a new, higher fade line with the #2 and start the band again
Take the line out with the trimmers, pressing them flat on the head
questions.why: A line is blended with an in-between length: the #1 with the lever open (or a #1.5), in short flicking strokes across the line itself. Cutting the whole upper band shorter just moves the line higher.

questions.q: The fade line is higher on the left than on the right. What is the best way to correct it?
o: Raise the right side to match, using the same point on each ear
Lower the left side by blending extra hair down into the #1 band
Leave it, because the line-up at the end will hide the small difference
Tilt Jaheim's head to the right while finishing the rest of the fade
questions.why: Hair cannot be put back, so the lower side is brought up to the higher one, a little at a time, using a fixed point on each side and checking from the front and the back. Then the plan is checked with the client, since the fade now sits slightly higher.

questions.q: Why did Kemar remove the bulk with the longest guard before he set the fade line?
o: A long guard keeps the blades cooler for the rest of the cut
The longest guard is the only one that cuts against the grain
The bottom bands must always be cut after the client has checked the top
A slip with a long guard still leaves hair to correct the mistake
questions.why: Working from long to short keeps your options open: if the first pass is uneven there is still length to fix it. Start short and a mistake cannot be undone.

questions.q: What should Kemar do about the two lines Jaheim wants cut in above his ear?
o: Cut them, since the client in the chair decides on his own style
Ask what his school allows and get his mother's agreement first
Refuse, because trainees must never cut lines or parts for anyone
Cut them faintly with a guard on, so that a teacher will not notice
questions.why: Jaheim is a minor and some schools do not allow parts or designs. The adult with him agrees the style, and a line cut into the hair cannot be removed before prize-giving.

questions.q: What should Akeem do about the bump with the yellow head near the left ear?
o: Squeeze it with gloved hands so that the trimmer can pass over it
Shave over it quickly with a fresh blade and apply styptic after
Leave that area uncut and suggest that Mr Stewart sees a doctor
Dab it with strong alcohol, then line the nape as he asked
questions.why: A swollen bump with pus is infected. Cutting over it or squeezing it spreads infection and causes scarring; a barber leaves the area alone and refers the client.

questions.q: Mr Stewart still wants 'skin at the back'. Which finish should Akeem offer for the nape instead?
o: A squared line cut one centimetre higher, above the bumps
The same skin finish, but cut with the trimmer and not a razor
A skin finish every week, so the hairs never grow long enough to curl
A soft taper left at a guard, cut with the grain, with no hard line
questions.why: On skin that forms bumps and raised scars, the hair is left slightly longer, cut with the grain, with a soft tapered edge. Cutting closer or more often is what causes the hairs to grow back into the skin.

questions.q: Why must Akeem keep the trimmer away from the thick, raised scar?
o: A fresh injury can make this kind of scar grow larger
Scar tissue blunts the trimmer blade within a few strokes
The scar is contagious and would infect the next client
Hair on a scar grows faster, so the line would not last
questions.why: Keloid-type scars grow in response to injury, so even a small nick can make them bigger. They are not contagious; the risk is to this client's own skin.

questions.q: Which note on Mr Stewart's record card will be most useful at his next visit?
o: 'Regular client. Usual cut. He was not happy about the back today.'
'Has a skin disease on his neck. Do not cut him until it is cured.'
'Bumps, raised scar at nape. Left at #1, tapered. Advised doctor.'
'Wanted skin at the back. Refused. Told him to change his collar.'
questions.why: A record states what was seen, what was done (with the guard) and the advice given, so any barber can repeat the safe cut. It does not diagnose a disease or record opinions.

questions.q: How should Monique deal with the matted hair at the back before she cuts?
o: Work it loose in small sections, starting from the ends
Wet the whole head thoroughly and comb it through from the roots
Cut the matted area out first, then shape the rest to match it
Run the clippers over it with the largest guard to break it up
questions.why: Mats are loosened a little at a time, from the ends towards the scalp, with fingers and a wide-tooth comb. Combing from the roots tears the hair, and cutting a mat out removes length the client asked to keep.

questions.q: Shantelle's hair stands higher on the right than on the left. What should Monique do first?
o: Cut the right side down until it matches the left side
Cut the left side first, as the shorter side sets the size
Ask Shantelle to tilt her head until both sides look level
Pick both sides out evenly, then judge again
questions.why: Hair that has been in braids or slept on is often flattened on one side. Until it is picked out evenly you cannot tell whether one side is really longer, and cutting on a guess makes the shape lopsided.

questions.q: Monique has cut the outline once round. The shape looks even. What should she do before she takes off any more?
o: Spray the hair with water so the coils tighten and show the shape
Pick the hair out again and look at it from a step or two back
Press the shape down with her palms to see where it is too full
Run a #8 guard over the whole head to level the surface
questions.why: Cutting and handling press coils down. Picking out again lifts hidden long hairs, and stepping back shows the whole outline, so she removes only what is needed and keeps the length Shantelle asked for.

questions.q: Which check tells Monique most about whether the finished afro is balanced?
o: Measuring one coil on each side with a ruler after stretching it
Asking Shantelle to feel both sides with her hands and compare
Looking from front, back and both sides with her head upright
Looking down on the top of the head while Shantelle bends forward
questions.why: Balance is judged by eye from every side, with the head level, comparing both sides in the mirror. A tilted or bent head, or a single measured coil, gives a false picture of the outline.

questions.q: Mrs Samuels will wear her hair curly. In what state should Kimone do the main shaping of the top?
o: Blown out as it is, because straight hair gives the cleanest line
Soaking wet, because wet hair is at its softest and easiest to cut
In its curly state, dry, after it has been washed and has reverted
Pressed flat with an iron, so that every hair is at full length
questions.why: Coily hair is shaped in the state the client will wear it. Hair cut while stretched looks even today but curls up shorter and often uneven after washing.

questions.q: Kimone's stretch test gives about 9 cm stretched and about 4 cm coiled. If she cut the blown-out top to 5 cm today, about how long would the curls look after washing?
o: About 5 cm, the same as the length that was cut
A little over 2 cm, under half the cut length
About 4 cm, the same as the test coil at the nape
About 9 cm, once the coils have had time to relax
questions.why: The test coil keeps a little under half its stretched length (4 out of 9). On that basis 5 cm of stretched hair would look only a little over 2 cm when curly, far shorter than the 5 cm of curl she wants.

questions.q: Mrs Samuels wants the cut done in one visit, today, while her hair is still straight. What is Kimone's best plan?
o: Cut the top to exactly 5 cm now, as that is the figure she gave
Refuse to cut at all today and tell her to come back with her hair washed
Cut the top to 5 cm, then press it again so it cannot shrink
Explain the shrinkage, leave the top longer, and refine it once curly
questions.why: The client must understand what will happen before any length comes off. Leaving the top long and finishing the shape once the hair has reverted protects her: more can be cut later, but length cannot be added back.

questions.q: The dropped clippers still run. What must Tyrese check before he uses them on a client?
o: That the battery or cord gives the same speed as it did before
That the moving blade has not shifted past the fixed blade
That the lever still moves freely from closed to open
That the body has not been scratched where his hand holds it
questions.why: A knock can push the blades out of line. If the cutting blade sits level with or past the fixed blade it will cut skin, so the blade setting, the teeth and the casing are checked after any drop.

questions.q: What should Tyrese do with the cracked #2 guard?
o: Use it for bulk only, where a small slip would not show
Tape the crack and use it until the shop buys a new set
Stop using it and replace it, although clients are waiting
Use the #3 guard with extra pressure to get nearly the same length
questions.why: A cracked guard can flex, slip off or let the blade through, leaving a bald strip or a cut. A queue of clients is not a reason to use damaged equipment.

questions.q: After the nick has been dealt with, what must happen to the trimmer before it touches anyone again?
o: It is wiped on the cape, then oiled so that the blade runs cool
It is brushed clean, then disinfected for the full contact time
It is sprayed with disinfectant at once, with the hair still in it
It is rinsed under the tap and left in the UV cabinet to dry
questions.why: Blood on a blade can carry infection to the next client. The hair and blood are removed first, because disinfectant cannot work through them, and then a suitable disinfectant is left on for the whole contact time on its label.

questions.q: A client with a round face and dense coily hair asks you to suggest a short style. Which usually suits him best?
o: An even round afro, the same length on the top and the sides
Fuller sides with the top cut low and flat to the head
A low cut on top with the sideburns left wide and full
Some height on top with the sides faded shorter
questions.why: Height on top and short sides make a round face look longer and slimmer. Fullness at the sides, or an evenly round shape, adds width and makes the face look rounder.

questions.q: A client brushes his low cut every day to form waves. How should you cut the top so the wave pattern is kept?
o: With the grain, using a low guard
Against the grain, with no guard
Scissor-over-comb on picked-out hair
In circles with a twist sponge first
questions.why: Waves are coils trained to lie flat in the direction of growth. Cutting with the grain shortens them without lifting or cutting out the pattern; cutting against it takes the waves off.
